Is juicing actually good for you?
A) Freshly juiced fruit has become a basic dietary item — especially for busy, health-conscious consumers who hope to save time preparing food while still getting nutrients. Fruit juice also has been linked to claims that it can help you both lose weight and stay healthy. All of which, of course, has made it highly profitable. The original article cited a 2016 global fruit and vegetable juice market estimate of $154 billion and expected further growth.
B) But is juicing really as healthy as we think? The effects of foods containing fructose—a naturally occurring sugar found in fruits and fruit juices—depend on the food and the overall diet. In whole fruit, fibre and intact cell structures help distinguish it from juice. It takes our digestive system a while to break these cells down and for fructose to enter the bloodstream.
C) Unlike whole fruit, strained fruit juice contains much less fibre. Sugars naturally present in fruit juice count as free sugars, along with added sugars and those in honey and syrups. WHO recommends keeping free sugars below 10% of daily energy intake, with a further reduction below 5% offering additional benefits. Separately, UK guidance recommends no more than 30g of free sugars daily for adults and a combined limit of 150ml a day for fruit juice, vegetable juice and smoothies. These are different measures: 150ml of juice is not equivalent to 30g of sugar. In a 2013 analysis of three US cohorts totalling 187,382 health professionals, greater fruit juice consumption was associated with a higher risk of type 2 diabetes. A 2008 study followed 71,346 female nurses for 18 years and also found an association. Such observational findings do not by themselves prove that juice causes diabetes; differences in fibre, food structure and other dietary factors may contribute.
D) Depending on the ingredients, vegetable juices may contain less sugar than fruit juices, but strained juices still lose much of the original fibre. Diets high in fibre have been linked to a lower risk of developing heart disease, stroke, high blood pressure and diabetes, and UK guidance recommends that adults consume 30g of fibre per day.
E) Aside from the link to type 2 diabetes, research raises concern about adverse effects when fruit juice adds excess calories. In a 2018 analysis of 155 controlled study comparisons, a team including John Sievenpiper, then an associate professor at the University of Toronto’s Department of Nutritional Sciences, set out to understand if the associations between sugary soft drinks and health — including risk of diabetes and heart disease — were applicable to the food and drink we generally consume as part of a healthy diet. He compared studies looking into the effects of fructose-containing sugars with control diets free from or lower in these sugars. His aim? To isolate the effects of consuming too many calories from the effects of foods containing different sugars.
F) The review found that effects depended on both energy intake and food source. Some fruit juice comparisons showed benefits for a blood-sugar measure when replacing other sources of calories, but adverse effects when juice added excess calories. Much of the evidence was of low certainty. Sievenpiper considered the UK daily juice limit of 150ml reasonable; the review did not establish that everyone should drink juice or that it prevents diabetes.
G) Fruit juice may contribute to excess energy intake, but the studies described here do not establish a simple rule that juice causes diabetes or that body weight alone determines its long-term effects. But we have a higher risk of consuming more than daily energy needs (which vary by person) on the days we drink juice, according to research. The article reports evidence that people do not always compensate for juice calories by eating less of other foods throughout the day.
H) As it is easy to consume large amounts of fruit juice quite quickly, extra calories are taken in. And extra calories can contribute to weight gain. Roger Clemens of the University of Southern California suggested choosing ripe fruit when making juice. Ripeness, however, does not restore the fibre lost in juicing or make juice a substitute for whole fruit.
I) Another reason for fruit juice’s recent popularity is the argument that it can help to remove poisonous or harmful substances from the body. However, “the whole concept of a juice diet helping to remove poisonous or harmful substances from the body is completely false,” says Clemens. Healthy organs normally process and remove many waste substances, but this does not mean the body can harmlessly eliminate every poison. There is no convincing evidence that commercial juice cleanses provide the advertised detoxification benefits.
J) And juice isn’t a cure-all for getting your nutrients, either. “There are a lot of nutrients contained in the parts of the fruits, such as in apple skins, that are excluded when you juice them,” says Heather Ferris, a professor of medicine. “You end up with sugary water with some vitamins.”
K) Plus, she adds, it’s not an ideal way to reach the advised ‘five a day’. “People try to get five servings of fruit and vegetables per day and don’t realise this isn’t just about getting vitamins,” she says. Whole fruits and vegetables contribute fibre and a range of nutrients to a balanced diet; this is not a general instruction to reduce all grains, protein and fats. A small serving of juice can supply some nutrients, but it does not replace the fibre and variety provided by whole fruit. The UK limit is 150ml of juice and smoothies combined per day, not 150ml of free sugars, and total energy intake also matters. It provides us with vitamins — but fruit juice is far from a quick fix.

研究说明：本文改编自穿衣心理学评论。2014 研究是 128 名男性的实验室谈判；2015 研究考察抽象加工，不是实际职场成功，也不支持一概宣称穿西装增加激素、穿便装更有创造力。社交着装建议属于作者观点。
We all take a little extra effort to look nice for special occasions. But most of us have conflicting feelings about dressing up and feel guilty about taking the time to focus on clothes. Some studies suggest the right dress may give us an extra edge in our professional and personal lives.
We hear sayings like “dress for the job you want, not the job you have”. Most people don’t really believe in them, but research into the impact of clothes on behavior now suggests that there may actually be a grain of truth in these sayings.
Research suggests that the clothes we wear can affect our behavior, our mood and even the way we interact with others because of the symbolic meaning that we assign to different types of clothing.
We consider some clothes to be powerful, some to be fun, and so on. We even evaluate people whom we have just met based on their clothes. We also evaluate ourselves based on what we are wearing because of the way they make us feel. This suggests that the experience of wearing something may affect our attitudes and our choice of behavior.
There’s a reason tailored jackets are associated with being “dressed for success”. It seems that wearing formal office wear puts us in the right frame of mind to conduct business. A 2014 laboratory experiment with 128 men found differences in negotiation outcomes and testosterone responses across clothing conditions. A separate 2015 series of studies linked formal clothing with more abstract processing. These findings do not show that a suit reliably raises everyone’s hormone levels or guarantees better work performance.
The author suggests that although formal clothing may suit some business situations, casual clothing may feel more appropriate for informal socializing. This is a contextual suggestion, not a universal rule that formal clothes make people unfriendly.
In the author’s view, a casual dress code may help some colleagues feel relaxed and approachable. This supports the author’s preference for business casuals on a Friday, but the appropriate choice depends on the workplace, occasion and wearer. The cited experiments do not establish that casual clothing generally makes people more creative.

阅读说明：本篇是关于古典音乐影响的评论。音乐表达力属于审美评价，现代音乐具有多种文化来源；已删除对青少年品味的一概判断和唯一源头说，第 52、54、55 题同步修订。
Alongside pop, jazz and electronic music, opera and classical music continue to compete for listeners’ attention. Some people are beginning to wonder whether opera and classical music are still relevant to the modern world of music. Listeners’ tastes vary, but the author sees several signs that opera and classical music remain relevant.
One indication of classical music’s continuing influence, the author argues, is that some popular music uses similar beats, harmonies, and melodies (旋律) as those that were used in some of classical music’s best works. Even so, it can be difficult for those who do not study music theory to see this as an indicator, since it is subtle and just shows the impact symphonic (交响乐的) orchestras have had on society’s taste in music.
A better example for the relevance of opera and classical music can be seen in the invention of the rock opera. Opera combines drama with music, usually through sung performance; telling stories in music is a broader practice shared by many traditions. The art of telling a story using music has not faded in the least bit. In fact, sometimes actual orchestras are used for major parts of the opera itself. Some of the world’s greatest hits have been parts of rock operas.
Fans of classical music can also tell you that there are few types of music that are more expressive. So, it should come as no surprise to anyone that classical music pieces are still used as background music in modern movies. Symphonic orchestra compositions have also been created solely for the purpose of being included in major motion pictures. These are often very well received amongst mainstream music fans.
Classical music and opera are among the influences on modern music, alongside African American and many other musical traditions. Given their continuing influence, the author expects them to remain important, though predictions about centuries to come are necessarily uncertain.

D) It contains elements similar to those in some masterpieces of classical music.

B) Many fans find them particularly expressive.
C) They are well received by movie fans from all over the world.
D) They are essential for movies to become the world’s greatest hits.

A) Classical music and opera are among its many influences.
B) It cannot outcompete classical music and opera in its impact on our current society.
C) It will not enjoy as much popularity as classical music and opera among music fans.
D) It might not be able to rival classical music and opera in importance for centuries to come.

Is juicing actually good for you?
A) Freshly juiced fruit has become a basic dietary item — especially for busy, health-conscious consumers who hope to save time preparing food while still getting nutrients. Fruit juice also has been linked to claims that it can help you both lose weight and stay healthy. All of which, of course, has made it highly profitable. The original article cited a 2016 global fruit and vegetable juice market estimate of $154 billion and expected further growth.
B) But is juicing really as healthy as we think? The effects of foods containing fructose—a naturally occurring sugar found in fruits and fruit juices—depend on the food and the overall diet. In whole fruit, fibre and intact cell structures help distinguish it from juice. It takes our digestive system a while to break these cells down and for fructose to enter the bloodstream.
C) Unlike whole fruit, strained fruit juice contains much less fibre. Sugars naturally present in fruit juice count as free sugars, along with added sugars and those in honey and syrups. WHO recommends keeping free sugars below 10% of daily energy intake, with a further reduction below 5% offering additional benefits. Separately, UK guidance recommends no more than 30g of free sugars daily for adults and a combined limit of 150ml a day for fruit juice, vegetable juice and smoothies. These are different measures: 150ml of juice is not equivalent to 30g of sugar. In a 2013 analysis of three US cohorts totalling 187,382 health professionals, greater fruit juice consumption was associated with a higher risk of type 2 diabetes. A 2008 study followed 71,346 female nurses for 18 years and also found an association. Such observational findings do not by themselves prove that juice causes diabetes; differences in fibre, food structure and other dietary factors may contribute.
D) Depending on the ingredients, vegetable juices may contain less sugar than fruit juices, but strained juices still lose much of the original fibre. Diets high in fibre have been linked to a lower risk of developing heart disease, stroke, high blood pressure and diabetes, and UK guidance recommends that adults consume 30g of fibre per day.
E) Aside from the link to type 2 diabetes, research raises concern about adverse effects when fruit juice adds excess calories. In a 2018 analysis of 155 controlled study comparisons, a team including John Sievenpiper, then an associate professor at the University of Toronto’s Department of Nutritional Sciences, set out to understand if the associations between sugary soft drinks and health — including risk of diabetes and heart disease — were applicable to the food and drink we generally consume as part of a healthy diet. He compared studies looking into the effects of fructose-containing sugars with control diets free from or lower in these sugars. His aim? To isolate the effects of consuming too many calories from the effects of foods containing different sugars.

Some fruit juice comparisons showed benefits for a blood-sugar measure when replacing other sources of calories, but adverse effects when juice added excess calories. Sievenpiper considered the UK daily juice limit of 150ml reasonable; the review did not establish that everyone should drink juice or that it prevents diabetes.
G) Fruit juice may contribute to excess energy intake, but the studies described here do not establish a simple rule that juice causes diabetes or that body weight alone determines its long-term effects. The article reports evidence that people do not always compensate for juice calories by eating less of other foods throughout the day.
